@@ -0,0 +1,127 @@
+    ZIP: Unassigned
+    Title: Limited Block Serving Service Flag
+    Owners: Marek <marek@zfnd.org>
+    Status: Draft
+    Category: Network
+    Created: 2026-11-03
+    License: MIT
+
+
+# Terminology
+
+The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", and "MAY" in this
+document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [^BCP14] when, and only
+when, they appear in all capitals.
+
+best tip
+:   The tip of a node's best block chain.
+
+limited peer
+:   A peer that advertises `NODE_NETWORK_LIMITED` and not `NODE_NETWORK`.
+
+
+# Abstract
+
+This ZIP defines the service flag `NODE_NETWORK_LIMITED` for the Zcash
+peer-to-peer protocol specified in ZIP 204 [^zip-0204]. A node that sets it
+serves at least the most recent 2,304 blocks of its best chain, but not
+necessarily older blocks. It is the Zcash counterpart of BIP 159
+[^bip-0159].
+
+
+# Motivation
+
+A node that deletes old block bodies, such as a Zebra node with pruning
+enabled, cannot set `NODE_NETWORK`, which promises the complete block chain.
+ZIP 204 defines no other flag for serving blocks, so such a node advertises no
+services. Peers then cannot tell that it can serve recent blocks: some do not
+use it to follow the chain tip, and others request historical blocks from it
+that it cannot serve.
+
+The Version 2 P2P protocol draft [^draft-p2p-v2] defines the same flag with
+the same window. This ZIP specifies it for the current protocol, so that it
+can be deployed without the other changes in that draft.
+
+
+# Specification
+
+## Service Flag
+
+The service flag `NODE_NETWORK_LIMITED` is defined as bit 10
+(`0x0000000000000400`) of the `services` field.
+
+A node that sets `NODE_NETWORK_LIMITED` MUST be able to serve every block of
+its best chain at a height greater than its best tip height minus 2,304, in
+response to `getdata` requests with `MSG_BLOCK`.
+
+A node that cannot serve the complete block chain MUST NOT set `NODE_NETWORK`.
+It SHOULD set `NODE_NETWORK_LIMITED` if it can meet the requirement above. A
+node that sets `NODE_NETWORK` MAY also set `NODE_NETWORK_LIMITED`.
+
+## Serving
+
+A limited peer SHOULD NOT serve blocks at heights more than 2,304 below its
+best tip, so that peers cannot infer how many blocks it retains. It MAY
+disconnect a peer that requests a block more than 2,306 blocks below its best
+tip; the 2-block margin allows for the best tip advancing while a request is
+in flight.
+
+## Requesting
+
+A node MUST NOT request a block from a limited peer if that block is more than
+2,304 blocks below the node's own best tip. A node SHOULD rely on limited
+peers for blocks only while its best tip is within 1,152 blocks of the
+network's best tip, leaving half of the window for chain reorganizations and
+for differences between the two nodes' best tips.
+
+## Address Relay
+
+Nodes SHOULD relay addresses advertising `NODE_NETWORK_LIMITED` as they relay
+other addresses.
+
+## Deployment
+
+This ZIP requires no network upgrade. Nodes ignore service flags they do not
+recognize, so a node can set `NODE_NETWORK_LIMITED` as soon as it implements
+this ZIP.
+
+
+# Rationale
+
+Bit 10 and the 2,304-block window match the Version 2 P2P protocol draft
+[^draft-p2p-v2], so a node can advertise the same capability in both
+protocols. Bit 10 is also the bit that BIP 159 assigns to the same capability
+in Bitcoin.
+
+The window is defined in blocks rather than time, so that a peer can check a
+request against it without knowing the block target spacing. At 75, 25 and 10
+seconds per block it covers about 48, 16 and 6.4 hours.
+
+The 1,152-block margin for requesters, and the rule against serving older
+blocks, follow BIP 159's 144-block reorganization buffer and its
+fingerprinting countermeasure. BIP 159 does not specify disconnection; the
+2-block margin follows Bitcoin Core's implementation [^bitcoin-core-limited].
+
+
+# Security and Privacy Considerations
+
+A limited peer that served all blocks it retains would reveal how many that
+is, which can help distinguish it from other nodes. Serving only the window
+avoids this.
+
+A node that relies only on limited peers cannot synchronize from more than
+2,304 blocks behind the tip. Nodes SHOULD keep connections to peers that set
+`NODE_NETWORK` while synchronizing.
+
+
+# References
+
+[^BCP14]: [Information on BCP 14 — "RFC 2119: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels" and "RFC 8174: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words"](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/bcp14)
+
+[^zip-0204]: [ZIP 204: Zcash P2P Network Protocol](zip-0204.rst)
+
+[^bip-0159]: [BIP 159: NODE_NETWORK_LIMITED service bit](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0159.mediawiki)
+
+[^draft-p2p-v2]: [Draft ZIP: Version 2 Zcash P2P Network Protocol](draft-arya-jvff-p2p-quic-transport.md)
+
+[^bitcoin-core-limited]: [Bitcoin Core: block requests below the NODE_NETWORK_LIMITED threshold (`net_processing.cpp`)](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/src/net_processing.cpp)

@@ -0,0 +1,529 @@
+    ZIP: Unassigned
+    Title: FROST Member Backup Strings for Shielded Zcash
+    Owners: Khadim <openpgp-wallet@protonmail.com>
+            aryaethn <aryaethn@gmail.com>
+    Credits: Hanh (hhanh00), for the zkfrost string in Zkool
+    Status: Draft
+    Category: Wallet
+    Created: 2026-10-26
+    License: MIT
+    Discussions-To: <https://github.com/zcash/zips/issues/1413>
+    Pull-Request: <https://github.com/zcash/zips/pull/1432>
+
+
+# Terminology
+
+The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "SHOULD", and "SHOULD NOT" in this document
+are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [^BCP14] when, and only when,
+they appear in all capitals.
+
+The terms "Mainnet" and "Testnet" in this document are to be interpreted as
+defined in the Zcash protocol specification [^protocol-networks].
+
+The terms below are to be interpreted as follows:
+
+Group
+
+: A set of $n$ participants holding a FROST threshold key for Orchard-protocol
+  spend authorization [^zip-0312], any $t$ of whom can sign.
+
+Member
+
+: One participant of a group, identified by its FROST identifier.
+
+Signing share
+
+: The member's secret share of the group's Spend authorizing key, as output
+  by key generation.
+
+Group verifying key, $\mathsf{ak}$
+
+: The FROST group public key, used as the Spend validating key
+  $\mathsf{ak}$ of the group's Orchard full viewing key. Its encoding has a
+  $\tilde{y}$ bit of $0$, as § 4.2.3 of the protocol specification requires
+  [^protocol-updated-orchardkeycomponents].
+
+$\mathsf{sk}$
+
+: The 32-byte value the members agree on during key generation, from which
+  the rest of the group's key components are derived [^zip-2005-usagewithfrost].
+
+Derivation
+
+: How $\mathsf{nk}$ and $\mathsf{rivk}$ are obtained from $\mathsf{sk}$ and
+  $\mathsf{ak}$. This ZIP knows two, defined in [Derivations].
+
+Member backup string
+
+: The string defined in this ZIP.
+
+
+# Abstract
+
+This ZIP defines a backup string for one member of a FROST group that spends
+shielded ZEC with Orchard-protocol keys (in the Orchard or Ironwood pool). The
+string holds the member's identifier, the threshold, the group size, the
+member's signing share and the group's $\mathsf{sk}$. Together with the group's
+unified full viewing key, it is enough to rebuild the member in any wallet that
+implements this ZIP, without the other members being online. Restoring checks
+the string against the viewing key, which both detects a string from another
+group and tells the wallet which key derivation the group uses.
+
+Version 1 of the payload is byte-for-byte the `zkfrost` string that Zkool
+already ships, so existing backups stay valid.
+
+The string is more sensitive than the signing share it carries: it also
+carries $\mathsf{sk}$, from which a holder can compute the group's quantum
+spending key $\mathsf{qsk}$ [^zip-2005]. It never appears on chain.
+
+
+# Motivation
+
+Several wallets now offer FROST groups for shielded ZEC: Zkool, Zafe,
+Konclave, and the Zcash Foundation's tools. Each one backs up its members in its
+own format, so a member can only restore their seat in the app that created
+it. In July 2026, Zkool's author described the situation: "There is no
+standard for it. I choose a way that makes it restorable on Zkool only. One
+day, someone will write a ZIP." [^zkool-forum]
+
+Since then, Zkool has moved to a minimal backup string (`zkfrost`, Zkool
+6.35.0) that holds only what a member needs. This ZIP takes that string as its
+first version, so that:
+
+- a user can move a seat from one wallet to another, or restore it in a
+  different app after losing a device;
+- a group can mix implementations, which avoids having every signer come from
+  one vendor;
+- funds stay reachable if one app is abandoned.
+
+ZIP 2005 adds a reason. To recover notes with the Recovery Protocol, "it is
+necessary to retain, or be able to rederive, $\mathsf{sk}$, and also to know
+whether $\mathsf{use\_qsk}$ was used to derive the $\mathsf{ivk}$ and
+addresses" [^protocol-updated-orchardkeycomponents]. A backup format is where
+that knowledge has to live.
+
+
+# Privacy Implications
+
+The string never leaves the member's custody in normal use and is not
+published on chain, so this ZIP changes nothing for on-chain privacy.
+
+Combined with the group's unified full viewing key, a string gives no viewing
+capability beyond what that viewing key already gives. Without the viewing
+key, $\mathsf{sk}$ yields $\mathsf{nk}$ but not the incoming viewing key, which
+also depends on $\mathsf{ak}$. The string does reveal $t$, $n$ and the member's
+identifier.
+
+A wallet that shows the string as a QR code exposes it to cameras and
+onlookers, as with any secret displayed on screen.
+
+
+# Requirements
+
+- A member can be rebuilt from its string and the group's unified full viewing
+  key, with no other member online.
+- A wallet detects a string that belongs to another group before using it.
+- The restore tells which derivation the group uses.
+- The format does not depend on how $\mathsf{sk}$ was agreed.
+- Backups made with Zkool's `zkfrost` string stay valid.
+- The format can gain new versions without breaking existing strings.
+
+
+# Non-requirements
+
+- Key generation, including how the members agree on $\mathsf{sk}$
+  [^zip-0312-key-generation].
+- Signing, and the transport between members.
+- Encryption of the string at rest (see [Open issues]).
+- A birthday height. zips#1401 proposes to carry it in the unified full
+  viewing key [^zips-1401], which the restore already needs.
+- Splitting $\mathsf{qsk}$ between members.
+- FROST groups using Sapling keys.
+
+
+# Specification
+
+## Derivations
+
+Let $\mathsf{H^{ask}}$, $\mathsf{H^{nk}}$, $\mathsf{H^{rivk}}$,
+$\mathsf{H^{qsk}}$, $\mathsf{H^{qk}}$ and
+$\mathsf{H}^{\mathsf{rivk\_ext}}_{\mathsf{qk}}$ be as defined in § 4.2.3
+of the protocol specification as updated by ZIP 2005
+[^protocol-updated-orchardkeycomponents].
+
+ZIP 2005 derivation
+
+: $\mathsf{nk} = \mathsf{H^{nk}}(\mathsf{sk})$, and
+  $\mathsf{rivk} = \mathsf{H}^{\mathsf{rivk\_ext}}_{\mathsf{qk}}(\mathsf{ak}, \mathsf{nk})$
+  where $\mathsf{qk} = \mathsf{H^{qk}}(\mathsf{H^{qsk}}(\mathsf{sk}))$. This is
+  the $\mathsf{use\_qsk} = \mathsf{true}$ branch that ZIP 2005 requires for
+  FROST [^zip-2005-usagewithfrost]. Notes received by such a group are
+  quantum recoverable.
+
+Legacy derivation
+
+: $\mathsf{nk} = \mathsf{H^{nk}}(\mathsf{sk})$ and
+  $\mathsf{rivk} = \mathsf{H^{rivk}}(\mathsf{sk})$, with the group verifying key
+  as $\mathsf{ak}$. Zkool created groups this way before supporting ZIP 2005.
+  Such a group follows neither branch of § 4.2.3
+  [^protocol-updated-orchardkeycomponents]: $\mathsf{ak}$ is not derived from
+  $\mathsf{sk}$, and $\mathsf{rivk}$ does not commit to a $\mathsf{qk}$. Notes
+  received by such a group are therefore not quantum recoverable.
+
+## Encoding
+
+A member backup string is the Bech32m [^bip-0350] encoding of a payload, with
+the human-readable part `zkfrost`. As in ZIP 316 [^zip-0316], the length limit
+of Bech32m is not applied; a version 1 string is 123 characters long.
+
+Encoders MUST produce lowercase strings. Decoders MUST accept a string that is
+entirely lowercase or entirely uppercase, and MUST reject a string in mixed
+case, as Bech32m requires. A wallet can still show the string in uppercase,
+for instance in a QR code (see [Rationale]), by converting it after encoding.
+
+The human-readable part is the same on Mainnet and Testnet, and the payload
+names no network: the network is given by the unified full viewing key used to
+restore. A string paired with another group's viewing key, on either network,
+fails the check in [Restore].
+
+## Payload, version 1
+
+| Offset | Size | Field |
+|--------|------|-------|
+| 0      | 1    | format version, $\mathtt{0x01}$ |
+| 1      | 1    | member identifier $i$ |
+| 2      | 1    | threshold $t$ |
+| 3      | 1    | group size $n$ |
+| 4      | 32   | signing share |
+| 36     | 32   | $\mathsf{sk}$ |
+
+The member's FROST identifier is the Pallas scalar with integer value $i$.
+The group size $n$ is the number of members.
+
+The signing share is the little-endian encoding of a Pallas scalar, as in the
+FROST(Pallas, BLAKE2b-512) ciphersuite [^zip-0312]. It MUST be the share that
+matches the $\mathsf{ak}$ in the group's viewing key. Key generation can output
+a group key with either $\tilde{y}$ bit; when it is $1$, the group key and
+every share are negated. The `reddsa` crate does this at the end of its key
+generation, and frost-client does it after the DKG. An implementation that
+skips this step would export a wrong share for about half of all groups.
+
+## Decoding
+
+A decoder MUST reject the string if any of the following holds:
+
+- it is not valid Bech32m, including a bad checksum, a Bech32 checksum, or
+  mixed case;
+- the bits left over when converting its data part to bytes are more than 4
+  or not all zero, as ZIP 173 requires [^zip-0173]. A version 1 string leaves
+  1 bit, so each payload has only one lowercase string;
+- its human-readable part, compared case-insensitively, is not `zkfrost`;
+- the format version is not $\mathtt{0x01}$;
+- the payload is not exactly 68 bytes long;
+- $n = 0$, $i = 0$, $i > n$, $t < 2$, or $t > n$. FROST needs at least two
+  signers.
+
+Checking the version before the length lets a decoder report a string of a
+later version as unsupported rather than as corrupt.
+
+## Restore
+
+The inputs are a member backup string and the group's unified full viewing
+key. The viewing key MUST contain an Orchard component (typecode
+$\mathtt{0x03}$ [^zip-0316]), which holds $\mathsf{ak}$, $\mathsf{nk}$ and
+$\mathsf{rivk}$. Ironwood uses the same Orchard-protocol keys.
+
+1. Decode the string as above.
+2. Reject the string if $\mathsf{sk}$ is not a valid Orchard spending key,
+   that is if $\mathsf{H^{ask}}(\mathsf{sk}) = 0$, or if the signing share is
+   not the canonical encoding of a Pallas scalar. (A group's $\mathsf{ask}$ is
+   not derived from $\mathsf{sk}$; the first check only keeps decoders in
+   agreement with the validity rule for Orchard spending keys.)
+3. Take $\mathsf{ak}$ from the viewing key. Compute $\mathsf{nk}$ and
+   $\mathsf{rivk}$ under each derivation of [Derivations].
+4. If the ZIP 2005 derivation gives the viewing key's $\mathsf{nk}$ and
+   $\mathsf{rivk}$, the group follows the ZIP 2005 derivation. Otherwise, if
+   the legacy derivation does, the group follows the legacy derivation.
+   Otherwise the wallet MUST reject the string: it belongs to another group.
+5. Rebuild the member's key material from the identifier, the signing share,
+   the threshold $t$ and $\mathsf{ak}$ as the group verifying key. If the
+   wallet knows the group's verifying shares, it SHOULD check that the
+   member's verifying share matches.
+
+A wallet SHOULD tell the user which derivation was found, and SHOULD warn when
+it is the legacy one, whose notes are not quantum recoverable.
+
+The check in step 4 proves that the viewing key was derived from the string's
+$\mathsf{sk}$, not that its $\mathsf{ak}$ is the group's (see
+[Security Considerations]). Before it shows an address to receive funds, a
+wallet SHOULD check the viewing key against a source the member trusts, such as
+the export made with its own string (see [Export]), an address of the group
+that the member recorded before and that the viewing key gives, or the same
+viewing key obtained from at least two other members. A member that lost its
+device may have lost its export too, and then has to ask the others for the
+key, which is the case the attack needs: if one of the members it asks is
+honest, a forged key shows up as a mismatch.
+
+After the restore, the wallet MUST retain $\mathsf{sk}$ when the group follows
+the ZIP 2005 derivation. ZIP 2005 makes $\mathsf{qsk}$, which is derived from
+$\mathsf{sk}$, essential for recovering the group's notes once the current
+Orchard protocol is disabled [^zip-2005-usagewithfrost], and the signing
+share and viewing key alone do not give it. A wallet SHOULD also retain
+$\mathsf{sk}$ for a legacy group, since without it the member cannot export
+its string again.
+
+A restored member holds no signing nonces. It MUST generate fresh ones for its
+next signing session.
+
+The check in step 4 proves $\mathsf{sk}$, not the signing share. A wrong share,
+such as one stored with the wrong sign, passes the restore and is caught at the
+member's first signing: the verifying shares of the $t$ signers, which travel
+with their commitments, interpolate to $\mathsf{ak}$ only if every one of them
+is right. The signing transport is out of scope for this ZIP, but a signing
+protocol used with these strings SHOULD carry each signer's verifying share,
+so that a member restored from a string is checked when it first signs.
+
+## Export
+
+A wallet that exports a member backup string SHOULD export the group's unified
+full viewing key with it, or tell the user that the restore needs it. ZIP 2005
+asks FROST members to retain the group verifying key $\mathsf{ak}$
+[^protocol-updated-orchardkeycomponents]; in version 1 it is only held by the
+viewing key.
+
+A wallet MUST NOT put signing nonces, or any other secret beyond the fields
+above, in a version 1 string.
+
+## Storage and transmission
+
+Wallets MUST protect every member backup string at least as securely and
+reliably as $\mathsf{ask}$, as ZIP 2005 requires of $\mathsf{qsk}$
+[^zip-2005-usagewithfrost], and not merely like one signing share.
+
+Wallets SHOULD NOT store or transmit a string encrypted only under public-key
+encryption based on discrete logarithms or on factoring, such as Orchard note
+encryption, X25519, or RSA and elliptic-curve OpenPGP keys.
+
+
+# Rationale
+
+**Bech32m.** It gives a checksum that catches copy errors and a string users
+can paste or show as a QR code. An uppercase string fits the QR alphanumeric
+mode, which makes the code smaller. Its checksum guarantees the detection of
+any error affecting at most 4 characters only for strings of at most 90
+characters [^zip-0173] [^bip-0350]. A version 1 string is 123 characters
+long, so it keeps the 30-bit checksum without that guarantee, as unified
+addresses and viewing keys do [^zip-0316].
+
+**No network in the string.** A member's share is the same on every network
+the group lives on. The viewing key carries the network.
+
+**$\mathsf{ak}$ is not stored.** The restore needs the viewing key anyway to
+scan the chain, and checking $\mathsf{nk}$ and $\mathsf{rivk}$ against it
+catches a string from another group. The cost is that the string does not
+authenticate $\mathsf{ak}$ (see [Security Considerations]).
+
+**$\mathsf{sk}$ is stored whole.** ZIP 2005 makes it necessary "to retain, or
+be able to rederive, $\mathsf{sk}$" [^protocol-updated-orchardkeycomponents],
+and every member already holds it, along with $\mathsf{qsk}$
+[^zip-2005-usagewithfrost].
+
+**The derivation is found, not recorded.** Version 1 is Zkool's existing
+payload, which has no field for it. With two derivations and the viewing key at
+hand, trying both is cheap and unambiguous: both matching would need a
+collision in the hash functions behind $\mathsf{rivk}$. A later version can
+record the derivation explicitly (see [Open issues]).
+
+**One-byte identifier.** It covers groups whose identifiers are the integers
+1 to $n$, as in Zkool and in frost-client's trusted-dealer key generation.
+frost-client's DKG and Zafe derive 32-byte identifiers, which need another
+version (see [Open issues]).
+
+**Version 1 is Zkool's payload.** Backups users already made keep working,
+and the first implementation exists today.
+
+
+# Security Considerations
+
+A string holds one signing share. Fewer than $t$ strings cannot spend, as long
+as discrete logarithms on the Pallas curve stay hard.
+
+Every string also holds $\mathsf{sk}$, which yields $\mathsf{qsk}$. ZIP 2005
+notes that "a quantum adversary may be able to steal the funds with only
+access to $\mathsf{qsk}$, which is held by every participant"
+[^zip-2005-usagewithfrost]. Against such an adversary the threshold may give no
+protection: one leaked string, from any member, may be enough to steal the
+funds. ZIP 2005 requires each participant to "treat $\mathsf{qsk}$ as a
+secret held at least as securely and reliably as $\mathsf{ask}$"
+[^zip-2005-usagewithfrost], which is why [Storage and transmission] asks the
+same for every string.
+
+For the same reason, a string that is stored or sent encrypted only under
+public-key encryption based on discrete logarithms or on factoring is exposed
+to an adversary who records the ciphertext now and gains a quantum computer
+later. A passphrase with a memory-hard KDF and an AEAD (see [Open issues])
+does not have this weakness.
+
+The restore does not prove the signing share (see [Restore]). A wrong share,
+for instance one exported with the wrong sign (see [Payload, version 1]),
+gives signature shares that fail verification. It stops that member from
+signing until it is restored from a correct string, but it cannot sign
+anything or leak the other shares.
+
+The restore does not authenticate $\mathsf{ak}$ either. Every member holds
+$\mathsf{sk}$, so a dishonest member can build a viewing key around another
+$\mathsf{ak}$, for instance one whose secret it holds alone, with the
+$\mathsf{nk}$ and $\mathsf{rivk}$ that either derivation gives for it. A string
+restored with that key passes every check in [Restore], and the wallet then
+shows addresses that only that member can spend from. The wallet would not see
+the group's notes, and the group's signatures would not verify under that
+$\mathsf{ak}$, but funds received at those addresses before anyone notices are
+lost to the group. Checking the viewing key against a trusted source, as
+[Restore] asks, prevents this; so would carrying $\mathsf{ak}$ in the string
+(see [Open issues]).
+
+A member restored from a string has the same authority as before: the string
+adds no signer to the group. It carries no nonces, so a restore cannot bring
+back a nonce that was already used or published.
+
+
+# Deployment
+
+This ZIP changes no consensus rule. Wallets can adopt it at any time.
+
+
+# Reference implementation
+
+- Zkool: `rust/src/frost/backup.rs` in hhanh00/zkool2, released in Zkool
+  6.35.0 [^zkool-backup].
+- frost-zec: `src/backup.rs` in OpenPGP-Wallet/frost-zec, by one of this
+  ZIP's owners, written from this ZIP's rules apart from Zkool's code, with
+  `backup export` and `backup restore` commands [^frost-zec-backup]. Its
+  `tools/zip-vectors` generates the test vectors below.
+
+
+# Test vectors
+
+The full set is in `draft-khadim-aryaethn-frost-member-backup/vectors.json`.
+It covers a 2-of-3 ZIP 2005 group, a 2-of-3 legacy group together with the
+ZIP 2005 viewing key built from the same $\mathsf{sk}$ and $\mathsf{ak}$ (whose
+strings restore under either key, with a different derivation), and a 3-of-5
+ZIP 2005 group; an uppercase string; seventeen strings that decoders must
+reject, two of them for the padding rule and one with a threshold of 1; and

+# Open issues
+
+- **Identifier encoding.** frost-client's DKG derives identifiers as
+  `Identifier::derive(session_id || pubkey)`, and Zafe from the vault id and
+  the member's identity key, so groups created by either use full 32-byte
+  identifiers (frost-client's trusted dealer uses 1 to $n$). For their groups
+  to fit, a version 2 needs a type byte followed by a short or a full
+  identifier.
+- **Identifiers after a refresh.** Refreshing shares to remove a member keeps
+  the other members' identifiers [^frost-refresh], so a group can end up with
+  identifiers 1, 2 and 4 and $n = 3$. Version 1 rejects member 4 ($i > n$), so
+  it covers only groups whose identifiers are 1 to $n$, which is what Zkool
+  creates. A version 2 could drop that check: the restore can match the
+  identifier against the group's verifying shares when it knows them.
+- **Explicit derivation.** A version 2 could record the derivation, so a
+  restore does not depend on trying each one, and a third derivation could be
+  added without ambiguity.
+- **Groups with no $\mathsf{sk}$.** zcash-sign's `generate`, which Konclave
+  uses, derives $\mathsf{nk}$ and $\mathsf{rivk}$ from a random $\mathsf{sk}$
+  and then discards it, so version 1 cannot hold its groups. A version 2 could
+  record that $\mathsf{nk}$ and $\mathsf{rivk}$ come from the viewing key,
+  leave $\mathsf{sk}$ out, and carry the viewing key itself (next item).
+  Carrying only $\mathsf{ak}$, as first suggested in zcash/zips#1413, would let
+  the restore catch a viewing key from another group, but not a different
+  viewing key for the same group. Such groups are not quantum recoverable
+  under ZIP 2005.
+- **The viewing key in the string**, so that a restore needs only the string.
+  For a group with no $\mathsf{sk}$, the viewing key is the only source of
+  $\mathsf{nk}$ and $\mathsf{rivk}$. A version 2 would carry the raw 96-byte
+  Orchard full viewing key rather than its unified encoding, so that the
+  string stays network-agnostic. With the viewing key in the string, nothing
+  outside it is left to mismatch. For a group with $\mathsf{sk}$,
+  $\mathsf{ak}$ is enough, since $\mathsf{nk}$ and $\mathsf{rivk}$ follow from
+  $\mathsf{sk}$ and $\mathsf{ak}$. Either way, $\mathsf{ak}$ would then come
+  from the member's own backup rather than from a viewing key obtained
+  elsewhere (see [Security Considerations]). A string for a group with no
+  $\mathsf{sk}$ would be about 230 characters long, or 280 with a 32-byte
+  identifier (see [Rationale] on Bech32m).
+- **Birthday height in version 2.** A raw Orchard full viewing key does not
+  carry the birthday height that zips#1401 would add to the unified encoding
+  [^zips-1401], so a string that restores on its own would need a birthday
+  field of its own, as Konclave noted in zcash/zips#1413. A height only means
+  something on one network, so the field would either name the network or
+  apply to the network the wallet restores on.
+- **Passphrase profile.** An optional version encrypting the payload with a
+  memory-hard KDF and an AEAD, as Zafe does for its backups.
+- **Human-readable part.** `zkfrost` is kept for compatibility with existing
+  backups. Should a later version use a more neutral one?

prs.title: [ZIP 316] Add Viewing Key Birthday Height metadata (Typecode 0xC0)
prs.author: nuttycom
prs.bodyExcerpt: Closes #1401 Assigns Typecode `0xC0`, the first Typecode in the non-MUST-understand Metadata range, to a Viewing Key Birthday Height Metadata Item: a little-endian `u32` giving the height of the first block that a user of the UFVK or UIVK should scan in order to detect funds. Specification summary:

files.patch:
From bca7aab74ab8e65a0e04f7fc5b1528d6a2740cd6 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Kris Nuttycombe <kris@nutty.land>
Date: Thu, 15 Oct 2026 15:29:33 -0600
Subject: [PATCH] ZIP 316: Add Viewing Key Birthday Height metadata (Typecode
 0xC0)

A wallet that imports a UFVK or UIVK must currently obtain the account's
birthday height out of band, or scan from a conservative default height.
This assigns Typecode 0xC0, from the non-MUST-understand Metadata range,
to a Metadata Item that carries the height of the first block that a user
of the viewing key should scan in order to detect funds.

The item is permitted only in UFVKs and UIVKs, is retained when deriving
a UIVK from a UFVK, and is omitted from derived Unified Addresses. Because
it is not MUST-understand, it may also appear in Revision 0 viewing keys,
and Consumers that do not recognise it ignore it. To keep such keys
usable for Revision 0 derivation, only MUST-understand Metadata Items now
force a derived UIVK or Unified Address to be Revision 2.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
---
 zips/zip-0316.rst | 103 ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++----
 1 file changed, 96 insertions(+), 7 deletions(-)

diff --git a/zips/zip-0316.rst b/zips/zip-0316.rst
index 0cec75c94..3fecefeb4 100644
--- a/zips/zip-0316.rst
+++ b/zips/zip-0316.rst
@@ -942,6 +942,89 @@ set this bound more tightly; a common expiry delta used by many wallets is 40
 blocks from the current chain tip, as suggested in ZIP 203
 [#zip-0203-default-expiry]_.
 
+Viewing Key Birthday Height Metadata
+------------------------------------
+
+Typecode $\mathtt{0xC0}$ is reserved for optional Viewing Key Birthday Height
+metadata. This Metadata Item Type is permitted only in Unified Full Viewing
+Keys and Unified Incoming Viewing Keys.
+
+The value of a $\mathtt{0xC0}$ item MUST be an unsigned 32-bit integer in
+little-endian order specifying the Birthday Height of the UFVK or UIVK: the
+height of the first block, on the Zcash chain associated with the UFVK or
+UIVK, that a user of the viewing key should scan in order to detect funds.
+
+A Producer MAY include a $\mathtt{0xC0}$ item in a UFVK or UIVK. A Producer
+SHOULD set the Birthday Height to a height no greater than the height of the
+earliest block that contains a transaction sending funds to any address
+derivable from the Items of the UFVK or UIVK.
+
+A Producer MUST NOT include a $\mathtt{0xC0}$ item in a Unified Address. A
+Consumer MUST ignore a $\mathtt{0xC0}$ item in a Unified Address.
+
+If a UFVK or UIVK contains both a $\mathtt{0xC0}$ item and a $\mathtt{0xE0}$
+item, then the Producer MUST ensure that the Birthday Height is less than or
+equal to the Address Expiry Height, and a Consumer MUST reject the UFVK or
+UIVK as invalid if the Birthday Height is greater than the Address Expiry
+Height.
+
+A Consumer that scans the chain to detect funds for a UFVK or UIVK that
+contains a $\mathtt{0xC0}$ item SHOULD begin scanning at the Birthday Height.
+The Consumer MAY begin scanning at a lower height. If the Consumer begins
+scanning at a greater height, then it might fail to detect funds.
+
+When deriving a UIVK from a UFVK that contains a $\mathtt{0xC0}$ item, the
+$\mathtt{0xC0}$ item MUST be retained unmodified in the derived UIVK.
+
+When deriving a Unified Address from a UFVK or UIVK that contains a
+$\mathtt{0xC0}$ item, the derived Unified Address MUST NOT contain a
+$\mathtt{0xC0}$ item.
+
+Rationale for Viewing Key Birthday Height Metadata
+''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''''
+
+.. raw:: html
+
+   <details>
+   <summary>Click to show/hide</summary>
+
+A wallet that imports a viewing key without a birthday height must either ask
+the user for one or scan from a conservative default, such as the activation
+height of the oldest shielded protocol that the viewing key supports. Scanning
+from such a default can take much longer than scanning from the actual
+birthday height. Carrying the birthday height in the viewing key removes this
+cost and the need for a separate channel to convey it. A Producer can also set
+a later Birthday Height when the earlier history of the viewing key is not
+relevant to its intended use.
+
+The birthday height is assigned a Typecode outside the MUST-understand range
+because a Consumer that ignores it remains correct: it scans from an earlier
+height, which costs time but cannot cause it to miss funds. A MUST-understand
+Typecode would instead require every existing Consumer to reject an otherwise
+usable viewing key, and would prohibit its use in `Revision 0`_ viewing keys.
+
+The birthday height describes a viewing key, not a payment destination. A
+Sender has no use for it, and including it in a Unified Address would reveal
+the approximate age of the recipient's wallet to every party that sees the
+address. It is therefore prohibited in Unified Addresses. A Consumer ignores
+such an Item instead of rejecting the address, because the Item does not
+affect how a Sender uses the Receivers of the address, and rejecting the
+address would not undo the information leak. A holder of a viewing
+key can already observe the heights of the transactions that the key detects,
+so including the birthday height in the viewing key reveals little additional
+information to such a holder.
+
+Each address derived from an expiring viewing key expires at or before the
+Address Expiry Height of the viewing key, so a conforming Sender will not send
+funds to it in a block above that height. A Birthday Height greater than the
+Address Expiry Height would direct the Consumer to begin scanning after all
+such transactions. Such a viewing key is inconsistent and is treated as
+invalid.
+
+.. raw:: html
+
+   </details>
+
 Typecode Registry
 -----------------
 
@@ -964,8 +1047,9 @@ transaction construction could result in additional information being leaked
 on-chain. As such a user giving out a ``tu`` address should recognise that
 they may be giving up some privacy in transactions received at that address.
 
-If a new Metadata Item type should not be allowed in ``zu`` addresses, it MUST
-be assigned in the MUST-understand Metadata range.
+If a new Metadata Item type is permitted in some Unified Addresses but should not
+be allowed in ``zu`` addresses, it MUST be assigned in the MUST-understand
+Metadata range.
 
 Experimental Typecodes ($\mathtt{0xFFFA}$ to $\mathtt{0xFFFF}$) are permitted
 at the discretion of wallets that have opted into the corresponding experiment
@@ -988,7 +1072,9 @@ properties of ``zu`` addresses.
   +-------------------+--------------------------------------+----+--------+--------+
   | 0x04..=0xBF       | Unassigned                           | ❌ | ❌     | ❌     |
   +-------------------+--------------------------------------+----+--------+--------+
-  | 0xC0..=0xDF       | Non-MUST-understand Metadata         | ❌ | ❌     | ❌     |
+  | 0xC0              | Viewing Key Birthday Height [2]      | ❌ | ❌     | ❌     |
+  +-------------------+--------------------------------------+----+--------+--------+
+  | 0xC1..=0xDF       | Unassigned Non-MUST-understand       | ❌ | ❌     | ❌     |
   +-------------------+--------------------------------------+----+--------+--------+
   | 0xE0              | Address Expiry Height                | ❌ | ✅     | ✅     |
   +-------------------+--------------------------------------+----+--------+--------+
@@ -1003,6 +1089,9 @@ properties of ``zu`` addresses.
 
 [1] See note above regarding experimental typecodes in ``zu`` addresses.
 
+[2] Permitted only in UFVKs and UIVKs, as specified in
+`Viewing Key Birthday Height Metadata`_.
+
 Additions to this registry are made via 2xxx-series ZIPs. This table will be
 updated by the ZIP Editors when such a ZIP transitions to ``Proposed`` status.
 
@@ -1083,8 +1172,8 @@ all "MUST-understand" Metadata Item Typecodes present in the UFVK in
 order to derive a UIVK from it.
 
 If the source UFVK is Revision 2 then the derived UIVK SHOULD be
-Revision 2; if the source UFVK includes any Metadata Items then
-the derived UIVK MUST be Revision 2.
+Revision 2; if the source UFVK includes any MUST-understand Metadata
+Items then the derived UIVK MUST be Revision 2.
 
 For Metadata Items recognised by the Consumer, the processing of the
 Item when deriving a UIVK is specified in the section or ZIP describing
@@ -1128,8 +1217,8 @@ all "MUST-understand" Metadata Item Typecodes present in the UIVK in
 order to derive a Unified Address from it.
 
 If the source UIVK is `Revision 2`_ then the derived Unified Address
-SHOULD be Revision 2; if the source UIVK includes any Metadata Items
-then the derived Unified Address MUST be Revision 2.
+SHOULD be Revision 2; if the source UIVK includes any MUST-understand
+Metadata Items then the derived Unified Address MUST be Revision 2.

To better reflect that focus an

@@ -0,0 +1,198 @@
+
+    ZIP: Unassigned
+    Title: Zcash Adoption Pool (ZAP)
+    Owners: Daira-Emma Hopwood <daira@jacaranda.org>
+    Credits: Violet Rollergirl
+             Blake Benthall (emersonian)
+             Mylo Bennett
+             Alison Stevenson
+    Status: Draft
+    Category: Consensus Process
+    Created: 2026-10-30
+    License: MIT
+    Discussions-To: <https://forum.zcashcommunity.com/t/zcash-adoption-pool-zap/58656>
+    Pull-Request: <https://github.com/zcash/zips/pull/1431>
+
+
+# Terminology
+
+The key words "MUST" and "SHALL" in this document are to be interpreted as
+described in BCP 14 [^BCP14] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.
+
+The terms "Mainnet" and "Testnet" in this document are to be interpreted as
+defined in the Zcash protocol specification [^protocol-networks].
+
+The terms "Zcash Community Grants" (or "ZCG"), "ZCG Committee", and "Deferred
+Dev Fund Lockbox" are to be interpreted as defined in ZIP 1015 [^zip-1015].
+
+The terms "Protocol-defined Ecosystem Funding" and "Coinholder-Controlled Fund"
+are to be interpreted as defined in ZIP 1016 [^zip-1016].
+
+“ZEC” refers to the native currency of Zcash on Mainnet.
+
+
+# Abstract
+
+Reaffirm the portion of Protocol-defined Ecosystem Funding allocated to
+Zcash Community Grants (ZCG), and focus on its original goal described in
+ZIP 1015 [^zip-1015-zcg] — to accelerate Zcash adoption as broadly as
+possible. To better reflect that focus and to clarify the original intent
+of ZIP 1015, this portion of funds will be called the "Zcash Adoption Pool".
+
+
+# Motivation
+
+As specified in ZIP 1015:
+
+> The stream allocated to Zcash Community Grants (ZCG) is intended to fund
+> independent teams entering the Zcash ecosystem, to perform major ongoing
+> development (or other work) for the public good of the Zcash ecosystem, to the
+> extent that such teams are available and effective. The ZCG Committee is given
+> the discretion to allocate funds not only to major grants, but also to a
+> diverse range of projects that advance the usability, security, privacy, and
+> adoption of Zcash, including community programs, dedicated resources, and other
+> projects of varying sizes.
+
+There is no shortage of projects that fulfil these criteria and that are in
+desperate need of funding.
+
+## Background
+
+Throughout the history of the Zcash project, there have been periodic calls to
+abandon support for independent teams entering the Zcash ecosystem. This has
+presented itself in a variety of forms with numerous arguments. At no point in
+Zcash's history, however, has there ever been a lack of use cases for programmes
+and initiatives that utilize shielded ZEC.
+
+Most recently, calls for the abolition of the ZCG have made absurd arguments,
+including that there is more money in the Zcash Community Grants portion of the
+"dev" fund than is required for "development". This argument presupposes that
+"development" should be limited to technical protocol development, which is a
+clear misinterpretation of both the letter of ZIP 1015 (as quoted above), and
+its original intent. That intent was not changed by ZIP 1016. Notably, these
+proposals have not stipulated any change to the Coinholder-Controlled Fund —
+which in practice would result in a substantial shift of power toward large
+holders.
+
+Another such argument is that development work can be funded via other means,
+such as private equity, and therefore "should" be funded by private equity. The
+authors of this ZIP do not object to funding from private equity. Rather, this
+ZIP reaffirms the utility of funding programmes that private equity has
+evidently *not* funded, and for which no other reliable source of funding
+currently exists.
+
+There are many programmes that may apply for ZCG grants whose source for funds
+is at risk, but for whom support will undeniably increase the adoption rate of
+Zcash. That is precisely what the "dev" fund was designed to fund.
+
+To clarify this in literal terms, this ZIP therefore renames the pool of funds
+and the grant programme funded via the `FS_FPF_ZCG_H3` slice of Protocol-defined
+Ecosystem Funding to explicitly include the word "adoption", in order to avoid
+further misinterpretation or the possibility of future misappropriation of the
+funds previously allocated for purposes of broader Zcash and ZEC adoption.
+
+
+# Requirements
+
+All requirements of ZIP 1015 continue to apply; in particular:
+
+* There is a well-defined, publically agreed, process for evaluation and
+  community feedback on grant proposals.
+* Any use of Deferred Dev Fund Lockbox funds is consistent with the purpose
+  specified in [^zip-1015-lockbox] of "funding grants to ecosystem participants".
+
+In addition:
+
+* Funds disbursed through the Zcash Adoption Pool are to be further disbursed for
+  the explicit purpose of increasing the number of human individuals who have
+  direct holdings in ZEC or who directly transact in ZEC on the Zcash network.
+  The purpose of this is to further broaden the holding of ZEC and increase the
+  velocity of its use as a currency. This is what *adoption* means.
+
+
+# Non-requirements
+
+* Pleasing everyone.
+
+
+# Specification
+
+For avoidance of doubt, the `FS_FPF_ZCG_H3` funding stream SHALL continue at its
+existing value and for the duration specified in ZIP 214 Revision 3 [^zip-0214].
+This applies to Mainnet and Testnet.
+
+The pool of funds associated with this stream SHALL be renamed to
+"Zcash Adoption Pool" ("ZAP"), and the grant programme by which it is disbursed
+to "Zcash Adoption Pool Grants" ("ZAP Grants"). Assets associated with Zcash
+Community Grants (past, present, or future) therefore become assets associated
+with the Zcash Adoption Pool; requirements on their administration specified in
+ZIPs 1015 and 1016 [^zip-1015] [^zip-1016] are unchanged. The ZCG Committee SHALL
+be referred to as the ZAP Committee.
+
+The ZAP Grant assessment process MUST obtain reasonable confidence, on the evidence
+in the application, that funds disbursed through Zcash Adoption Pool Grants will
+be further disbursed for the explicit purpose of increasing the number of human
+individuals who have direct holdings in ZEC or who directly transact in ZEC on the
+Zcash network. The purpose of this is to further broaden the holding of ZEC and
+increase the velocity of its use as a currency.
+
+## Examples
+
+Examples of end-recipients who might receive ZEC as a result of grants approved
+under this programme include:
+
+* sex workers who are debanked or require electronic payment means otherwise
+  unavailable to them, and their clients that require payment discretion;
+* civil society organizations who struggle to maintain funding;
+* privacy projects and contributors in need of legal defence;
+* technical development projects that would similarly struggle to
+  receive funding from private investments (a past example would be Arti, an
+  implementation of Tor in Rust);
+* people protesting surveillance or restrictions on their speech, movement, and
+  freedom of association;
+* abortion funds;
+* people in need of humanitarian aid and disaster relief, e.g. across borders;
+* communities threatened by genocide or forced displacement;
+* debanked individuals;
+* remittance recipients;
+* victims of abuse;
+* homeless people;
+* trans people attempting to access hormones;
+* refugees;
+* people unable to obtain food or medical care due to discrimination;
+* people in need of education in underfunded nations;
+* publishers catering to underserved groups or to political views opposing
+  discrimination;
+* projects developing accessibility features, or localization to minority
+  languages;
+* small businesses choked by excessive payment processing fees;
+* people and businesses unable to access the financial system due to payment
+  processor discrimination and censorship.
+
+Some of these examples are intentionally provocative. All can be funded
+entirely legally in most jurisdictions. They are presented here to highlight
+the requirement that Zcash remain **for everyone**.
+
+
+# Acknowledgements
+
+The authors would like to thank the attendees of the Zcon7 conference for
+discussions leading to this proposal, and the organizers of the conference
+for the space to discuss it in person.
+
+
+# References
+
+[^BCP14]: [Information on BCP 14 — "RFC 2119: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels" and "RFC 8174: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words"](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/bcp14)
+
+[^protocol-networks]: [Zcash Protocol Specification, Version 2026.8.0 [NU6.3]. Section 3.12: Mainnet and Testnet](protocol/protocol.pdf#networks)
+
+[^zip-0214]: [ZIP 214: Consensus rules for a Zcash Development Fund](zip-0214.rst)
+
+[^zip-1015]: [ZIP 1015: Block Subsidy Allocation for Non-Direct Development Funding](zip-1015.rst)
+
+[^zip-1015-zcg]: [ZIP 1015: Block Subsidy Allocation for Non-Direct Development Funding — Zcash Community Grants](zip-1015#zcash-community-grants-zcg)
+
+[^zip-1015-lockbox]: [ZIP 1015: Block Subsidy Allocation for Non-Direct Development Funding — Lockbox](zip-1015#lockbox)
+
+[^zip-1016]: [ZIP 1016: Community and Coinholder Funding Model](zip-1016.md)

prs.title: Add draft ZIP: Wallet-to-Wallet Messaging
prs.author: arya2
prs.bodyExcerpt: Adds `zips/draft-arya-wallet-to-wallet-messaging.md`, a Standards / Wallet draft specifying an off-chain, mailbox-based channel between wallets over an anonymity network: - Envelopes are encrypted to the Orchard Receiver of the recipient's Unified Address, reusing the Orchard key agreement with a do

files.patch:
@@ -0,0 +1,677 @@
+    ZIP: Unassigned
+    Title: Wallet-to-Wallet Messaging
+    Owners: Arya <arya@zfnd.org>
+    Status: Draft
+    Category: Standards / Wallet
+    Created: 2026-11-03
+    License: MIT
+    Pull-Request: <https://github.com/zcash/zips/pull/???>
+
+
+# Terminology
+
+The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", and "MAY" in this
+document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [^BCP14] when, and only
+when, they appear in all capitals.
+
+The terms "Unified Address", "Unified Viewing Key", "Receiver", "Metadata
+Item", "Typecode", "Producer", and "Consumer" are to be interpreted as defined
+in ZIP 316. [^zip-0316] An "Orchard Receiver" is a Receiver with Typecode
+$\mathtt{0x03}$.
+
+compactSize
+
+: A variable-length integer as used in the Bitcoin protocol,
+  [^Bitcoin-CompactSize] in minimal encoding, with a value of at most
+  $\mathtt{0x02000000}$.
+
+Sender wallet
+
+: The wallet that creates and deposits an Envelope.
+
+Recipient wallet
+
+: The wallet an Envelope is encrypted to.
+
+Envelope
+
+: An encrypted message, padded to a size class, as deposited in a Mailbox.
+
+Mailbox
+
+: A service that holds Envelopes for a Recipient wallet until it fetches them.
+
+Mailbox Descriptor
+
+: The data a Sender wallet needs to deposit an Envelope in a Mailbox.
+
+Transport Binding
+
+: A specification of the Mailbox operations over one anonymity network,
+  identified by a `binding_id`.
+
+Payload
+
+: The typed content carried inside an Envelope.
+
+
+# Abstract
+
+This ZIP specifies an off-chain channel between Zcash wallets. A Sender wallet
+that holds a Recipient wallet's Unified Address deposits an encrypted Envelope
+in a Mailbox over an anonymity network, and the Recipient wallet fetches it
+later. Neither wallet reveals its network identity to the other, and the
+Mailbox operator does not learn who sent an Envelope.
+
+Envelopes are encrypted to the Orchard Receiver of the Unified Address, using
+the Orchard key agreement with a domain-separated key derivation, so no new
+keys have to be exchanged. A new ZIP 316 Metadata Item carries the Mailbox
+Descriptor in the Unified Address. Payload types are defined for
+acknowledgements, text, ZIP 321 payment requests, and PCZTs, with codes
+reserved for FROST signing rounds and off-chain note delivery. Mailbox
+credentials are derived from the wallet seed with ZIP 32 registered key
+derivation.
+
+Anyone who holds the recipient's Orchard incoming viewing key can read its
+Envelopes, and a Mailbox Descriptor links every Unified Address that carries
+it. Transport Bindings are specified separately; Appendix A sketches one for
+the Nym mixnet. [^nym]
+
+
+# Motivation
+
+Several wallet protocols need a direct channel between wallets. Each wallet
+that wants one currently builds its own, so wallets from different vendors
+cannot talk to each other:
+
+- Multisig and hardware-signer flows pass PCZTs [^pczt] between parties.
+- FROST signing (ZIP 312 [^zip-0312]) runs over a confidential, authenticated
+  channel between the Coordinator and the signers whose mechanism ZIP 312
+  leaves out of scope. This ZIP supplies the confidential, anonymous
+  transport; a FROST payload would have to carry its own authentication.
+- Payment requests (ZIP 321 [^zip-0321]) and acknowledgements have no
+  wallet-to-wallet transport.
+- Project Tachyon [^tachyon] [^tachyon-post] proposes removing in-band secret
+  distribution from transactions, which makes an off-chain delivery channel a
+  requirement rather than an add-on.
+
+On-chain memos are the only standard channel today. ZIP 231 [^zip-0231]
+proposes to lift their 512-byte size cap, but memos would still cost fees, be
+stored by every full validator forever, and need a block confirmation per
+round, which rules out interactive protocols such as PCZT and FROST
+exchanges.
+
+ZIP 324 [^zip-0324] delegates delivery to a channel the parties already
+share, such as a secure messenger or a QR code, for the case where the sender
+has no address for the recipient. It does not help when the sender does hold
+a Unified Address, which is the case this ZIP covers.
+
+The idea is not new. Hornby's 2020 light wallet privacy review [^hornby-2020]
+lists out-of-band transaction delivery over a mixnet as an option and notes
+that scalable Zcash will need a mixnet or similar technology anyway. zips#629
+[^zips-629] suggests a mixnet plus a "private mailbox" to keep offline
+reception. The Nym × Zcash integration guide [^nym-zcash] covers routing a
+wallet's chain-sync and transaction-submission traffic through the mixnet,
+not wallet-to-wallet delivery. This ZIP fills that gap.
+
+
+# Privacy Implications
+
+**Who can read Envelopes.** Envelopes are encrypted to an Orchard Receiver, so
+anyone holding the account's Orchard incoming viewing key can decrypt them.
+That is the trust model of incoming notes, but Envelopes can carry more: a
+PCZT reveals a transaction the recipient is about to sign, including its
+outputs. Users who share incoming viewing keys with auditors or watch-only
+services should not expect Envelopes to be private from them.
+
+**Linkability.** A Mailbox Descriptor is a stable identifier. Two Unified
+Addresses that carry the same descriptor are linked to one recipient by anyone
+who sees both, which defeats diversified addresses. Unlinkable addresses
+therefore need separate mailboxes, at the cost of more credentials to derive
+and more mailboxes to fetch from. A `reply_to` address inside an Envelope has
+the same property for the sender.
+
+**Network observers and the Mailbox operator.** The anonymity network hides
+the sender's network identity from the operator and the recipient, and the
+recipient's from the sender. The operator still sees how many Envelopes a
+mailbox receives, their size classes, and when they are deposited and
+fetched. In bindings where the recipient connects to its own mailbox
+directly, as in the Nym sketch of Appendix A, the operator also learns the
+recipient's network identity unless the connection is tunnelled, for example
+over Tor. Network privacy is only as good as the anonymity set: while few
+wallets use a binding, cover traffic carries most of the weight.
+
+**Timing.** A deposit made at the same moment as a related on-chain
+broadcast, a fetch triggered by opening the app, or an immediate
+acknowledgement each leak timing that an observer can correlate with chain
+activity. The wallet behaviour rules in the specification reduce but do not
+remove this.
+
+**No sender authentication and no forward secrecy.** Envelopes do not
+authenticate their sender, so a Text payload can impersonate anyone; the
+specification forbids presenting it as coming from a named party. Envelope
+keys derive from long-lived keys, so compromise of an incoming viewing key
+exposes every Envelope the adversary has recorded, as for on-chain notes.
+
+**Denial of service.** Anyone holding a Unified Address can fill its mailbox.
+The cost falls on the mailbox's storage and the recipient's bandwidth; trial
+decryption itself is cheap. Bindings are expected to document quotas, and the
+unencrypted Envelope header lets a wallet see size classes before fetching
+bodies where a binding allows that.
+
+
+# Requirements
+
+- A sender holding only a recipient's Unified Address can deliver a message
+  with no prior contact.
+- The recipient need not be online when the message is sent.
+- No long-term key material is needed beyond what the wallet derives from its
+  seed, and a wallet restored from seed can recover its mailboxes on a
+  best-effort basis.
+- Neither the Mailbox operator nor a network observer learns the sender's
+  network identity or links a sender to a recipient. The sender does not learn
+  the recipient's network identity.
+- An Envelope reveals nothing about its content beyond its size class.
+- Wallets that implement ZIP 316 but not this ZIP can still parse and pay a
+  Unified Address that carries a Mailbox Descriptor, provided the Typecode
+  registration requested in the Specification is granted.
+- The core protocol does not depend on any one network or token.
+
+
+# Non-requirements
+
+- Sender authentication at the Envelope layer. Payload types that need it
+  carry their own.
+- Guaranteed delivery. Delivery is best-effort; protocols built on top have to
+  handle loss.
+- Forward secrecy.
+- Group messaging.
+- Hiding the recipient's network identity from its own Mailbox operator. A
+  binding may provide this, and a wallet can add Tor, but the core does not
+  require it.
+
+
+# Specification
+
+## Overview
+
+    Sender wallet                                        Recipient wallet
+         |                                                      ^
+         | 1. read Orchard Receiver and Mailbox                 |
+         |    Descriptor from the recipient's UA                |
+         | 2. build and encrypt the Envelope                    | 5. trial-decrypt
+         | 3. Deposit over the anonymity network                |    with ivk
+         v                                                      |
+      [ Mailbox ] -------------- 4. Fetch over the anonymity network
+
+## Mailbox Descriptors [mailbox-descriptors]
+
+A Mailbox Descriptor is encoded as:
+
+| Field            | Type                   | Description                      |
+|------------------|------------------------|----------------------------------|
+| `binding_id`     | `u16` (LE)             | Identifies the Transport Binding |
+| `descriptor_len` | `compactSize`          | Length of `descriptor`           |
+| `descriptor`     | `byte[descriptor_len]` | Binding-specific bytes           |
+
+Registered `binding_id` values:
+
+| `binding_id`                        | Binding                                      |
+|-------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
+| $\mathtt{0x0000}$                   | Reserved                                     |
+| $\mathtt{0x0001}$                   | Nym mixnet (Appendix A, non-normative)       |
+| $\mathtt{0xFF00}$–$\mathtt{0xFFFF}$ | Experimental; MUST NOT be used in production |
+
+## Unified Address Metadata Item [metadata-item]
+
+This ZIP defines a ZIP 316 Metadata Item, **Mailbox Descriptors**, with a
+Typecode in the Non-MUST-understand Metadata range $\mathtt{0xC0}$ to
+$\mathtt{0xDF}$, to be assigned by the ZIP Editors. [^zip-0316-metadata]
+
+The Item's value MUST parse as one or more Mailbox Descriptors, concatenated
+with no trailing bytes, in the recipient's order of preference. Descriptors
+with an unrecognised `binding_id` MUST be skipped, not rejected. A Sender
+wallet SHOULD use the first descriptor whose binding it supports.
+
+A Unified Address that carries this Item MUST also carry an Orchard Receiver;
+Envelopes are encrypted to that Receiver. The Item MUST NOT appear in a
+Unified Viewing Key.
+
+A Mailbox Descriptor is a stable identifier. A wallet MUST NOT put the same
+descriptor into two Unified Addresses that the user expects to be unlinkable.
+Wallets SHOULD include the Item only in addresses generated for a purpose
+that calls for messaging, and SHOULD NOT include it by default.
+
+If a binding's descriptors can go stale (for example in Appendix A, when the
+recipient changes gateway), the wallet SHOULD also set an Address Expiry Time
+Metadata Item [^zip-0316-expiry] on the address. Address Expiry Typecodes are
+MUST-understand, so such an address can only be paid by Consumers that
+implement ZIP 316 Revision 2; see [Open issues](#open-issues).
+
+### Typecode registration [typecode-registration]
+
+The ZIP 316 Typecode Registry [^zip-0316-registry] does not currently permit
+Producers to include Non-MUST-understand Metadata in any address type, and
+additions to the registry are made by 2xxx-series ZIPs. This ZIP requests the
+following row, to be applied when it reaches Proposed status:
+
+| Typecode | Description         | R0 | R2 `zu` | R2 `tu` |
+|----------|---------------------|----|---------|---------|
+| TBD      | Mailbox Descriptors | ✅ | ✅      | ✅      |
+
+The Item has no effect on transaction construction, so it meets ZIP 316's
+condition for `zu` addresses. Permitting it in Revision 0 addresses is what
+lets wallets that predate this ZIP pay the address, because Consumers ignore
+Items with Typecodes they do not recognise. If the ZIP Editors permit it only
+in Revision 2 addresses, the compatibility requirement holds only for
+Consumers that implement ZIP 316 Revision 2.
+
+## Envelope encryption [envelope-encryption]
+
+Let $(\mathsf{d}, \mathsf{pk_d})$ be the recipient's Orchard Receiver. Let
+$\mathsf{KA^{Orchard}}$ [^protocol-orchardkeyagreement],
+$\mathsf{DiversifyHash^{Orchard}}$ [^protocol-diversifyhash],
+$\mathsf{repr}_{\mathbb{P}}$ and $\mathsf{abst}_{\mathbb{P}}$
+[^protocol-pallasandvesta], and $\mathsf{ivk}$
+[^protocol-orchardkeycomponents] be as defined in the Zcash Protocol
+Specification, and let $\mathsf{LEBS2OSP}_{256}$ be used to encode Pallas
+points as 32-byte strings as in $\mathsf{KDF^{Orchard}}$.
+[^protocol-orchardkdf]
+
+The sender:
+
+1. Computes $\mathsf{g_d} = \mathsf{DiversifyHash^{Orchard}}(\mathsf{d})$.
+2. Chooses $\mathsf{esk}$ uniformly at random from
+   $\mathsf{KA^{Orchard}.Private}$. $\mathsf{esk}$ MUST NOT be reused across
+   Envelopes.
+3. Computes $\mathsf{epk} = \mathsf{KA^{Orchard}.DerivePublic}(\mathsf{esk}, \mathsf{g_d})$,
+   $\mathsf{sharedSecret} = \mathsf{KA^{Orchard}.Agree}(\mathsf{esk}, \mathsf{pk_d})$,
+   and $\mathsf{ephemeralKey} = \mathsf{LEBS2OSP}_{256}(\mathsf{repr}_{\mathbb{P}}(\mathsf{epk}))$.
+4. Derives the 32-byte key
+
+   $\hspace{2em}\mathsf{K} = \mathsf{BLAKE2b\text{-}256}(\texttt{"Zcash\_WalletMsg\_"}, \mathsf{LEBS2OSP}_{256}(\mathsf{repr}_{\mathbb{P}}(\mathsf{sharedSecret})) \,||\, \mathsf{ephemeralKey})$
+
+   This is $\mathsf{KDF^{Orchard}}$ with a different personalization, so
+   Envelope keys are domain-separated from note encryption keys even though
+   they share the key agreement.
+5. Chooses the smallest size class (see [Envelope format](#envelope-format))
+   whose padded size $N$ fits the plaintext, and pads the plaintext with zero
+   bytes to exactly $N$ bytes.
+6. Computes
+
+   $\hspace{2em}\mathsf{C} = \mathsf{IETF\_AEAD\_CHACHA20\_POLY1305.Encrypt}(\mathsf{K}, \mathsf{nonce}, \mathsf{aad}, \mathsf{plaintext})$
+   [^RFC8439]
+
+   with $\mathsf{nonce} = [\mathtt{0x00}]^{12}$ and
+   $\mathsf{aad} = \mathtt{version} \,||\, \mathtt{size\_class} \,||\, \mathsf{ephemeralKey}$.
+   The zero nonce is safe because $\mathsf{K}$ is unique to each
+   $\mathsf{esk}$.
+
+The recipient, for each Orchard incoming viewing key $\mathsf{ivk}$ it holds:
+
+1. Computes $\mathsf{epk} = \mathsf{abst}_{\mathbb{P}}(\mathsf{ephemeralKey})$
+   and rejects the Envelope if the result is $\bot$ or the identity
+   $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}$.
+2. Computes $\mathsf{sharedSecret} = \mathsf{KA^{Orchard}.Agree}(\mathsf{ivk}, \mathsf{epk})$.
+   Since $\mathsf{pk_d} = \mathsf{KA^{Orchard}.DerivePublic}(\mathsf{ivk}, \mathsf{g_d})$,
+   this equals the sender's value.
+3. Derives $\mathsf{K}$ as above and attempts decryption with the same
+   $\mathsf{aad}$. On failure, the Envelope is not for this key.
+4. Rejects the plaintext if it does not parse as described in
+   [Plaintext format](#plaintext-format), or if any padding byte is nonzero.
+5. Rejects the Envelope unless the plaintext's $\mathsf{d}$ is the
+   diversifier of an address of this account that this wallet issued either
+   with a Mailbox Descriptors Item or as a `reply_to`.
+
+A wallet processes an Envelope under the first $\mathsf{ivk}$ for which
+decryption succeeds. Steps 1 and 2 cost one point decompression and one
+scalar multiplication per Envelope and account.
+
+## Envelope format [envelope-format]
+
+| Field          | Type           | Description                                                             |
+|----------------|----------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
+| `version`      | `byte`         | $\mathtt{0x01}$                                                         |
+| `size_class`   | `byte`         | See table below                                                         |
+| `ephemeralKey` | `byte[32]`     | $\mathsf{LEBS2OSP}_{256}(\mathsf{repr}_{\mathbb{P}}(\mathsf{epk}))$     |
+| `ciphertext`   | `byte[N + 16]` | AEAD output; $N$ is set by `size_class`                                 |
+
+| `size_class`    | Padded plaintext size $N$ | Intended use              |
+|-----------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
+| $\mathtt{0x00}$ | 2048 bytes                | Acks, URIs, short text    |
+| $\mathtt{0x01}$ | 32768 bytes               | Small PCZTs, FROST rounds |
+| $\mathtt{0x02}$ | 262144 bytes              | Large PCZTs               |
+
+Other values are reserved. Recipients MUST reject Envelopes with an unknown
+`version` or `size_class`, or whose length does not match `size_class`.
+
+## Plaintext format [plaintext-format]
+
+| Field          | Type                | Description                                                   |
+|----------------|---------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
+| `payload_type` | `u16` (LE)          | See [Payload types](#payload-types)                           |
+| `flags`        | `byte`              | Bit 0: `ack_requested`; see below                             |
+| `d`            | `byte[11]`          | Diversifier of the Orchard Receiver the Envelope was sent to  |
+| `message_id`   | `byte[32]`          | Uniformly random                                              |
+| `in_reply_to`  | `byte[32]`          | `message_id` of the Envelope this one answers, or all zero    |
+| `expiry_time`  | `u64` (LE)          | Unix seconds; $0$ means no expiry                             |
+| `reply_len`    | `compactSize`       | Length of `reply_to`                                          |
+| `reply_to`     | `byte[reply_len]`   | A Unified Address, or empty                                   |
+| `payload_len`  | `compactSize`       | Length of `payload`                                           |
+| `payload`      | `byte[payload_len]` | Type-specific                                                 |
+| `padding`      | `byte[]`            | Zero bytes up to $N$                                          |
+
+Senders MUST set bits of `flags` other than bit 0 to $0$; recipients MUST
+ignore bits they do not recognise.
+
+`d` lets the recipient attribute the Envelope to one of its addresses without
+trusting `reply_to`, and `in_reply_to` lets protocols with several rounds
+match answers to requests.
+
+`reply_to`, if present, is the UTF-8 string encoding of a Unified Address
+[^zip-0316-encoding] whose Human-Readable Part matches the network of the
+Envelope's recipient. It MUST carry an Orchard Receiver and MAY carry a
+Mailbox Descriptors Item. A reply is encrypted to
+that Receiver. It is deposited in the mailbox named by the Item if there is
+one, or sent by a transport-level anonymous reply if the binding provides one
+(see [Mailbox operations](#mailbox-operations)); if neither is available, no
+reply is possible. A sender that wants replies without linking them to its
+other addresses SHOULD use a Unified Address and mailbox dedicated to replies.
+
+Senders SHOULD round `expiry_time` to the hour, to avoid leaking clock skew.
+
+Recipients:
+
+- MUST drop Envelopes whose `expiry_time` is nonzero and in the past.
+- MUST drop Envelopes whose `message_id` they have already processed, and
+  SHOULD remember processed `message_id`s at least until their expiry, or for
+  a wallet-chosen period when `expiry_time` is $0$.
+- MUST ignore the payload of an Envelope with an unknown `payload_type`, but
+  still record its `message_id`.
+
+## Payload types [payload-types]
+
+| `payload_type`                      | Name            | Payload                                                |
+|-------------------------------------|-----------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
+| $\mathtt{0x0000}$                   | Reserved        | —                                                      |
+| $\mathtt{0x0001}$                   | Ack             | Empty; `in_reply_to` names the acknowledged Envelope   |
+| $\mathtt{0x0002}$                   | Text            | UTF-8 text for display to the user                     |
+| $\mathtt{0x0003}$                   | Payment request | UTF-8 ZIP 321 URI [^zip-0321]                          |
+| $\mathtt{0x0004}$                   | PCZT            | Serialized PCZT [^pczt]; format reference TBD          |
+| $\mathtt{0x0005}$                   | Reserved        | FROST round messages (ZIP 312 [^zip-0312]); format TBD |
+| $\mathtt{0x0006}$                   | Reserved        | Off-chain note delivery [^tachyon]; format TBD         |
+| $\mathtt{0xF000}$–$\mathtt{0xFFFF}$ | Experimental    | MUST NOT be used in production                         |
+
+An Ack MUST NOT set `ack_requested`.
+
+Payloads MUST NOT carry spend authority, such as spending keys or ZIP 324 URIs
+[^zip-0324], because every holder of the recipient's incoming viewing key can
+read them.
+
+Payload types that cause side effects SHOULD carry their own replay
+protection; `message_id` deduplication and `expiry_time` only bound replay.
+
+## Mailbox operations [mailbox-operations]
+
+A Transport Binding MUST provide these operations:
+
+- **Deposit**(descriptor, envelope): deliver an Envelope to the Mailbox named
+  by the descriptor.
+- **Fetch**(credential) → envelopes: retrieve held Envelopes.
+- **Delete**(credential, handles): remove fetched Envelopes, unless the
+  binding documents that Fetch removes them implicitly.
+
+A Transport Binding MUST hide the sender's network identity from the Mailbox
+operator and from the recipient, and MUST hide the recipient's network
+identity from the sender. It SHOULD hide the recipient's network identity from
+the Mailbox operator, and SHOULD resist timing correlation by a global
+passive adversary. Bindings SHOULD rate-limit Deposit and SHOULD bound the
+storage a mailbox can consume.
+
+A Transport Binding specification MUST state:
+
+- the descriptor encoding;
+- how the 64-byte mailbox key from
+  [Mailbox key derivation](#mailbox-key-derivation) is turned into the
+  binding's credentials;
+- the retention period, or how a wallet learns it;
+- per-mailbox storage quotas, if any;
+- which size classes it supports;
+- how replies work: by depositing to a `reply_to` mailbox, by a
+  transport-level anonymous reply, or both, and how long each path stays
+  usable;
+- rate limiting and cost, if any;
+- what network identity, timing, and size information each party can
+  observe.
+
+## Mailbox key derivation [mailbox-key-derivation]
+
+Mailbox credentials are derived from the wallet seed $S$ with ZIP 32
+registered key derivation [^zip-0032-registered], using
+$\mathsf{ContextString} = \texttt{"Zcash\_WalletMessaging"}$ and
+$\mathsf{ZipNumber}$ equal to the number assigned to this ZIP:
+
+- $(\mathsf{sk}_{subtree}, \mathsf{c}_{subtree}) = \mathsf{RegKD}(\mathsf{ContextString}, S, \mathsf{ZipNumber})$
+- $(\mathsf{sk}_{n}, \mathsf{c}_{n}) = \mathsf{CKDreg}((\mathsf{sk}_{subtree}, \mathsf{c}_{subtree}), \mathsf{coin\_type} + 2^{31}, [\,])$
+- $(\mathsf{sk}_{b}, \mathsf{c}_{b}) = \mathsf{CKDreg}((\mathsf{sk}_{n}, \mathsf{c}_{n}), \mathtt{binding\_id} + 2^{31}, [\,])$
+- $(\mathsf{sk}_{a}, \mathsf{c}_{a}) = \mathsf{CKDreg}((\mathsf{sk}_{b}, \mathsf{c}_{b}), \mathsf{account} + 2^{31}, [\,])$
+- $\mathsf{K}_{i} = \mathsf{derive\_child\_cryptovalue}((\mathsf{sk}_{a}, \mathsf{c}_{a}), i + 2^{31}, [\,])$
+
+where $\mathsf{coin\_type}$ is the ZIP 32 coin type of the network
+[^zip-0032-paths], so that Mainnet and Testnet mailboxes are unlinkable;
+$\mathsf{account}$ is the ZIP 32 account index of the Orchard key whose
+addresses carry the descriptor; and $i$ is a per-binding, per-account counter
+that the wallet increments for each new mailbox. $\mathsf{K}_{i}$ is 64
+bytes; each binding states how it is split into credentials.
+
+A wallet restored from seed can rebuild its credentials by scanning $i$ from
+$0$ with a gap limit, subject to the binding's own limits (for example,
+knowing which gateway each mailbox used).
+
+## Wallet behaviour [wallet-behaviour]
+
+Sending:
+
+- Wallets SHOULD NOT deposit an Envelope at the same moment as a related
+  on-chain broadcast, and SHOULD add a random delay when the use is not
+  interactive.
+- Wallets MUST NOT fall back to a direct connection to a Mailbox when the
+  binding's anonymity network is unavailable.
+
+Fetching:
+
+- Wallets SHOULD fetch on a randomized schedule that does not depend on user
+  actions, including when no message is expected.
+- Wallets SHOULD cap the bytes they fetch and trial-decrypt per Fetch.
+
+Acknowledgements:
+
+- Wallets SHOULD send an Ack only when `ack_requested` is set, and SHOULD
+  delay it by a random amount.
+
+Display:
+
+- Envelopes are not authenticated. Wallets MUST NOT present a message as
+  coming from a named party unless the payload type itself authenticates the
+  sender, and SHOULD NOT open links in Text payloads without user
+  confirmation.
+
+Viewing keys:
+
+- Wallets that export an account's incoming viewing key to a third party
+  SHOULD NOT advertise mailboxes on that account's addresses.
+
+
+# Rationale
+
+**Why reuse Orchard key agreement?** It needs no new keys and no prior
+contact: any Unified Address with an Orchard Receiver is already a public
+encryption key. The cost is that incoming viewing key holders can read
+Envelopes; a dedicated messaging key in the descriptor would avoid that at
+the cost of a larger Item.
+
+**Why fixed size classes?** Exact lengths would leak payload types and
+content. Three classes keep the anonymity set per class large while still
+allowing PCZTs.
+
+**Why no ZIP 324 payload?** A sender that can use this channel already holds
+the recipient's Unified Address and can pay it on chain, and a ZIP 324 URI
+carries spend authority that every incoming viewing key holder could use.
+
+**Why a transport-agnostic core?** Tying a standard to one network and its
+token is a long-term risk. Nym is sketched first because it is live,
+packet-based, uses cover traffic, stores messages for offline clients, and
+offers sender-anonymous replies.
+
+
+# Reference implementation
+
+None yet.
+
+
+# Open issues [open-issues]
+
+- Assignment of the Metadata Item Typecode, whether it is permitted in
+  Revision 0 addresses, and this ZIP's number, which the key derivation
+  depends on.
+- Whether to encrypt to a dedicated messaging key carried in the descriptor
+  instead of to the Orchard Receiver, so that incoming viewing key holders
+  cannot read Envelopes.
+- Address Expiry Items make an address unpayable by ZIP 316 Revision 0
+  Consumers, while the compatibility requirement assumes they can pay it.
+  Whether to recommend expiry, shorter-lived descriptors, or neither.
+- The cost of running one mailbox per unlinkable address, and whether wallets
+  should offer a deliberately linkable "contact" mode.
+- A stable reference for the PCZT serialization.
+- The FROST round message format and its authentication layer.
+- The off-chain note delivery format, to be aligned with Tachyon.
+- Support for Sapling-only recipients.
+- A Tor onion-service binding.
+- Whether the Nym binding in Appendix A becomes normative in this ZIP or in a
+  separate one, once its TBDs are resolved.
+
+
+# Appendix A: Nym transport binding (non-normative) [nym-binding]
+
+This appendix sketches a binding for the Nym mixnet so that the core protocol
+can be evaluated against a real network. It is not a complete Transport
+Binding specification: the items marked TBD have to be resolved before it can
+be made normative. `binding_id` $\mathtt{0x0001}$ is reserved for it.
+
+**Descriptor.** The 96-byte binary form of a Nym client address,
+[^nym-addressing] [^nym-recipient] laid out as follows:
+
+| Field                 | Type       | Description                       |
+|-----------------------|------------|-----------------------------------|
+| client identity key   | `byte[32]` | Ed25519 public key                |
+| client encryption key | `byte[32]` | X25519 public key                 |
+| gateway identity key  | `byte[32]` | Ed25519 public key of the gateway |
+
+**Credentials.** The first 32 bytes of $\mathsf{K}_{i}$ would be the Ed25519
+seed of the client identity key, and the last 32 bytes the X25519 secret key
+[^RFC7748] of the client encryption key. The Nym Rust SDK accepts externally
+supplied client keys through a custom key store. [^nym-sdk-keys]
+
+**Deposit.** The sender sends the Envelope as a Nym message to the
+descriptor's address through the mixnet, from an ephemeral Nym client with
+fresh keys rather than from its own mailbox client, attaching reply SURBs
+[^nym-surbs] if it expects a prompt reply. Each ephemeral client has to
+register with an entry gateway and hold bandwidth credentials; the cost and
+latency of doing so per message are unverified (TBD).
+
+**Fetch.** The recipient runs a Nym client with the derived keys, connected to
+the gateway named in the descriptor, with cover traffic on. The gateway stores
+messages while the client is offline and delivers them when it connects.
+[^nym-addressing]
+
+**Delete.** Implicit on delivery by the gateway (TBD: confirm).
+
+**Retention.** Not documented by Nym (TBD).
+
+**Size classes.** All. Nym splits a message into fixed-size Sphinx packets,
+so larger classes take more packets and leave a larger timing footprint.
+
+**Replies.** SURB reply keys expire after 24 hours, [^nym-surbs] so SURBs
+serve interactive exchanges only. A recipient that fetches later can reply
+only to a `reply_to` address that carries a Nym descriptor.
+
+**Rate limiting and cost.** Sending through Nym consumes bandwidth
+credentials. Who pays, and whether they can be bought with shielded ZEC, is
+TBD.
+
+**Gateway changes.** The gateway is part of the descriptor. If the recipient
+moves gateway, old descriptors stop working and a new Unified Address has to
+be issued. How a wallet restored from seed learns which gateway each mailbox
+index used is TBD.
+
+**Observability.** The recipient's gateway, which is the Mailbox operator,
+sees the recipient's connection, including its IP address unless the
+connection is tunnelled over Tor, and the count and size of stored messages.
+The sender's entry gateway sees the sender's IP address but not the
+destination. Mix nodes see packets only. A global passive adversary faces
+Nym's mixing delays and cover traffic.
+
+
